# Will I be better off turning the start stop function off?

The decision to disable engine auto-stop in a modern vehicle like your 2017 VW Polo isn't just about personal preference; it's a calculation of thermodynamics versus fuel consumption. For drivers primarily engaged in short journeys under half an hour, the answer depends heavily on how often you encounter traffic lights or stop signs that force a complete halt.

When the engine cuts off at a red light, the vehicle relies entirely on the 12V auxiliary battery for electrical loads: power windows, infotainment systems, heated seats, and most critically, the Start-Stop system's own readiness logic. The moment you release the brake pedal or shift into Drive, the battery must deliver enough current to spin the starter motor, which requires a massive surge of powerâoften 150 to 200 ampsâfor a split second to crank the internal combustion engine back up.

This creates a specific thermal bottleneck. If your daily commute consists of a series of green lights or short distances where you don't actually stop, the battery spends most of its time in a state of low charge. The alternator, which charges the battery while driving, has to work harder to replenish the capacity lost during those frequent cranking events. In many modern ECUs, if the battery voltage drops below a certain threshold (often around 12.0V to 12.4V depending on the specific VW powertrain), the Start-Stop system will disengage automatically to protect the electrical architecture.

For short trips, this "charge-deep-discharge" cycle can be detrimental. The alternator takes roughly 3 to 5 minutes of steady driving to fully recharge a deep-discharged battery. If your journey is consistently under 10 minutes and you are stop-starting frequently, the battery never reaches full capacity before you arrive home or park for the night. Over time, this accelerates sulfation in lead-acid batteries or degrades Lithium-ion health faster than normal wear and tear.

There is also the issue of component lifespan. The starter motor is a robust piece of hardware, but it is designed for occasional use, not hundreds of cycles per day. Each cranking event subjects the starter solenoid and the flywheel teeth to mechanical stress. If you are turning the system off, you are effectively trading a small amount of immediate fuel savings (which might be negligible on short trips anyway) against extended battery life and reduced mechanical wear on the starter motor.

From a software engineering perspective, think of the Start-Stop feature as an aggressive optimization algorithm that runs only when specific conditions are met. If the "context" of your journeyâshort duration, frequent stopsâis unfavorable for the algorithm's goal (maximizing efficiency), disabling it prevents the system from entering an unstable state where it constantly toggles between running and stopping without achieving net energy gains.

If you decide to turn the feature off via the dashboard button or disable it in the car's settings menu, you are prioritizing electrical system stability over marginal fuel economy. Given that short journeys often involve cold engine conditions where catalytic converters need heat to become efficient anyway, the extra fuel consumed by keeping the engine running might actually be less than the cost of recharging the battery after every stop.

For a 2017 VW Polo, which likely uses an AGM (Absorbent Glass Mat) or EFB (Enhanced Flooded Battery), these batteries are more sensitive to deep discharge cycles than standard lead-acid units. Disabling the Start-Stop function ensures that the battery maintains a healthier state of charge throughout your daily short trips, potentially extending the service life of the 12V system significantly compared to leaving it active.
